docs.text.standard_statement: GlucoCraft sets no targets or ranges and makes no assessments. Every target and range shown is either taken from the cited published sources (consensus statements, studies and manufacturer documentation), each named as what it is — consensus: ranges and targets {cite:battelino2019}, tight range {cite:battelino2023}, CV ({ref:battelino2019}; the study by {ref:monnier2017}); studies: GMI {cite:bergenstal2018}, GRI {cite:klonoff2023}; manufacturer: trend categories {cite:abbott} — or set by the user in GlucoCraft's settings. Where GlucoCraft applies a rule of its own (for example the length of a data gap, or when a direction is called Stable), it is labeled as a GlucoCraft rule. GlucoCraft is designed to calculate and display; it sends notifications, prints reports and saves PDF and CSV files only as chosen in its settings or requested by the user. Where colors or the words met / not met appear, they are arithmetic comparisons with the cited target or the custom goal, not clinical assessments.
docs.text.limit_responsibility: It is the user's responsibility to know their CGM system and to adjust these settings where necessary.
docs.text.limit_note: The sensor limits must match the CGM sensor's measurement range. GlucoCraft sets them from the source where it can and shows a Repairs notice when the readings point to a different limit; otherwise they are set by hand (see {sec:lohi|Readings Outside the Sensor's Range (LO / HI)}). {limit_responsibility}
docs.text.interval_note: GlucoCraft is designed for readings every 5 minutes or more often. With 15-minute or longer intervals, the trend arrow, the 5-minute delta, the no-current-data limit, gaps and sensor active are not designed to function as described; readings are still stored and shown.
docs.text.sensor_active_note: Close to, but not the same as, the CGM system's own figure: only the readings received are counted.
docs.text.gap_rule: an interval between two readings that is longer than 15 minutes or three reading intervals, whichever is longer
docs.text.custom_note: The defaults are the international consensus ranges and targets {cite:battelino2019}. Ranges and goals that differ from them are custom settings.
docs.text.gmi_mmol_rule: GMI in mmol/mol is calculated from the mean glucose as 12.71 + 4.70587 × mean glucose in mmol/L {cite:bergenstal2018}, as a whole number, in the same way on every surface; the GMI goal (always entered in %) is converted in the same way, as the GMI in mmol/mol of the mean glucose whose GMI in % is the goal; laboratory A1C results entered in % are converted with the IFCC–NGSP master equation, mmol/mol = 10.929 × (% − 2.15) {cite:hoelzel2004} (both calculated by GlucoCraft).
docs.text.no_default_goals: The goals for time in tight range and for GMI have no default value: no goal is set until the user enters one in the settings, because no published target exists for them in clinical care (time in tight range: an aim for clinical trials only {cite:battelino2023}; GMI: no standardized goal {cite:ada2026|Table 6.2}).
docs.ranges.in_use_consensus: The settings contain the consensus ranges by default and may be changed; the consensus ranges are in use.
docs.ranges.in_use_custom: The settings contain the consensus ranges by default and may be changed; custom ranges are in use.
docs.colors.head.band: Graph range color (the graph's range bands)
docs.colors.range.near_low: In range, below the tight range
docs.colors.range.near_high: In range, above the tight range
docs.colors.caption_consensus: Shown with the ranges and colors currently in use: the consensus ranges {cite:battelino2019} and the tight range {cite:battelino2023}.
docs.colors.caption_custom: Shown with the ranges and colors currently in use: the custom ranges in the settings.

docs.section.essentials.title: Essentials
docs.section.essentials.body: • The sensor limits must match the CGM sensor's measurement range. GlucoCraft sets them from the source where it can and shows a Repairs notice when the readings point to a different limit; otherwise they are set by hand (Documentation: Readings Outside the Sensor's Range).
• GlucoCraft is designed for readings every 5 minutes or more often. The CGM systems and phone health apps that cannot deliver that are listed under Sources not supported for live display.

• Deleting GlucoCraft deletes every CSV (comma-separated values) export, and also its stored readings when When GlucoCraft is deleted is set to Delete everything (by default they are kept for a reinstall). To keep the readings, export them and copy the export files out of the glucocraft_exports folder before deleting; they can be read back in after a reinstall. With either choice, deleting GlucoCraft also deletes every report PDF and the recorded history and long-term statistics of its entities in Home Assistant's recorder.
• Data source. GlucoCraft does not communicate with a CGM sensor. It reads the Home Assistant entities selected in its settings, which are provided by another integration.
• Versions. Features, entity identifiers and settings may change between versions.
docs.section.how.title: How GlucoCraft Is Designed
docs.section.how.body: Overview

GlucoCraft is a Home Assistant integration. It is designed to read the selected glucose entity (and, where configured, a second glucose entity and a sensor-expiry entity), store each reading in Home Assistant, calculate statistics and trends, and display them on this dashboard, on the GlucoCraft display card and, where the user has built and connected them, on GlucoCraft wall panels (optional; see {sec:privacy|Privacy and Wall Panels}). {sources_in_use}

Calculations

GlucoCraft's results are its own calculations from the readings it receives, according to the rules and cited sources described in this Documentation; they are not the results of the CGM system or of its manufacturer's software.
Readings
<ul>

• Unit. Glucose entities report values in mg/dL or mmol/L, stated by their unit of measurement. A unit is read as mg/dL from mg/dL, mg/deciliter or mg/decilitre and as mmol/L from mmol/L, mmol/liter or mmol/litre, in any case; an entity that states any other unit (for example °F or %) cannot be chosen as a source, and a source that later states one is not used and raises the repair notice Glucose source with a unit other than mg/dL or mmol/L. A value without a unit is read as mg/dL; from such a source, values below 30 are not stored, and after 10 such values in a row a repair notice states that they indicate mmol/L. This method is a GlucoCraft rule. GlucoCraft stores and calculates in mg/dL and displays the unit selected in the settings (in use: {unit}). The glucose sensors use Home Assistant's blood glucose device class: Home Assistant converts their states and long-term statistics. The Display unit setting ({screen_units}) changes all GlucoCraft glucose sensors at once; a unit chosen for sensor.glucocraft_last_glucose_reading in Home Assistant's entity settings is applied to the others. The dashboard, the display card, the wall panels, the report and the notifications show the unit of sensor.glucocraft_last_glucose_reading. Changing the unit does not change the stored data, which GlucoCraft keeps in mg/dL. Home Assistant's own history graph (the history of a sensor and the History page) shows earlier values in the unit in which they were recorded until they are removed (after 10 days by default); this is Home Assistant behavior for every sensor. Conversion: 1 mmol/L = 18.016 mg/dL (molar mass of glucose 180.16 g/mol); mmol/L values are shown with one decimal, and halves are rounded away from zero everywhere. The consensus thresholds are shown with their published values in both units {cite:battelino2019}; the statistics are calculated with the mg/dL thresholds and are therefore the same in both units. A reading from a source in mg/dL is classified on its mg/dL value and shown rounded to 0.1 mmol/L, so 181 mg/dL is shown as 10.0 mmol/L and is high, and 141 mg/dL as 7.8 mmol/L and in range outside the tight range.

• Measurement time. Each reading retains its measurement time when the source entity provides it as an attribute. GlucoCraft recognizes the attribute names measurement_timestamp, dateString, date, timestamp, last_reading and reading_time, or the name set in its settings. A new value within 15 seconds of a stored reading counts as the same measurement and replaces it, so a source that updates faster than that adds no readings to the history (a repair notice says so after at least 10 minutes). With a second source, once the reading intervals of both sources are known, a value from the primary source counts as the same measurement within half the shorter of the two intervals (at least 15 seconds). Without such an attribute, the time of receipt in Home Assistant is used. A measurement time without a time zone is read in Home Assistant's time zone, so a source (for example a phone) set to another time zone can make its readings look early (a measurement time later than Home Assistant's clock is stored as the time the reading arrives); times on the dashboard, the display cards and the wall panels are in Home Assistant's time zone.

• Readings and no readings. A state that is not a glucose measurement is not stored: unavailable, unknown, ???, an empty state, values of 0 or less, and the error codes and warm-up markers of particular systems and integrations (listed in {sec:lohi|Readings Outside the Sensor's Range (LO / HI)}). A reading below or above the sensor's measurement range (LO / HI) gives no value and is stored as a limit reading (see {sec:lohi|Readings Outside the Sensor's Range (LO / HI)}). This method is a GlucoCraft rule.

• Two sources (optional). A second source is designed to supply readings that the primary source misses, up to 24 hours back, and to continue when it stops, merged by measurement time. Each measurement is stored once, and the primary source's value takes precedence. A reading measured more than 24 hours before both the current time and the newest stored reading is not stored, from either source; only the history import (at a start with fewer than 100 readings stored) and the CSV import (the action glucocraft.import_csv, see {sec:retention|Data Kept and CSV Export}) reach further back. A second source without measurement times is used only after the primary source has reported no reading for 5 minutes or three of its reading intervals, whichever is longer.
• Reading interval. GlucoCraft determines each source's reading interval from its most recent readings (in use: {interval}). {interval_note} See {sec:gaps|Gaps, Reading Interval and No Current Data}.

• History import. When GlucoCraft has fewer than 100 readings stored (a new installation, or after a damaged readings file), it imports the primary source's earlier states from Home Assistant's recorder when it starts, with the same rules as live readings, as far back as the recorder keeps them (10 days by default in Home Assistant) and at most {retention} days. With more readings stored (readings kept from an earlier installation, or after a time in which GlucoCraft was not loaded), it imports at each start the readings recorded after the newest stored one. In both cases a value without its own measurement time is left out when it may be the one Home Assistant writes again as the source comes up at a start. The second source is not imported. A reading that a source writes again with an unchanged value and unchanged attributes is not recorded by Home Assistant as a new row and cannot be imported: for a source without its own measurement time, a stretch of the same value (a steady value, or a time at LO or HI) comes in as its first reading followed by a gap, so the imported history can show less sensor active and a shorter time at the sensor's limit than the source had. This method is a GlucoCraft rule.
Status
<ul>

• No current data. No current data means that the newest reading is older than the limit set under No current data after ({screen_sources}; 5 to 30 minutes, default 15 minutes; in use: {stale} minutes), that there is no reading yet, or that the newest reading is more than 5 minutes later than the system clock. The trend arrow, the 5-minute delta and the in-range sensors are then shown as unknown; the display card and the wall panels show the words No current data in place of the glucose value, never a number, with the last reading and when it was taken under them, and the age of the last reading in the status bar (Reading: --- while the newest reading's time is more than 5 minutes ahead of the clock, because its age is then not known); graphs show a gap and percentages exclude the time only when the interval exceeds the gap rule. What the screens show, the optional notice, and why 15 minutes: see {sec:gaps|Gaps, Reading Interval and No Current Data}.

• Sensor expiry (optional). Read from the selected expiry entity: a date and time, a date (the start of that day, local time), a time stamp, or the time remaining in days, hours or minutes (a whole number of days: to the end of the local day that many days from today). Expiring soon: within 24 hours. Expired: the expiry time has passed, also while readings still arrive, until a later expiry time is received; the status then shows Sensor expired in red. Some CGM systems continue to deliver readings after the stated expiry: while readings still arrive, the value and its zone word keep their zone color, the trend follows the readings, and the red status bar of the display card and the wall panels shows Sensor expiry passed, which fades in and out until a new sensor is recognized (see {sec:gaps|Gaps, Reading Interval and No Current Data}). GlucoCraft does not observe the sensor itself, only the stated expiry. A Repairs notice says when the expiry entity does not exist (CGM sensor expiry entity not found), when it has held a value that is no expiry at its last 10 checks, over about 50 minutes (CGM sensor expiry entity holds no expiry), or when it gives an expiry more than a day past while readings still arrive (CGM sensor expiry entity shows an expiry long past); each closes by itself when the cause is gone or the setting is changed.

• Sensor warm-up. A new sensor is recognized when the expiry moves more than one day later, or when the source sends a warm-up marker. The warm-up ends with the first reading measured after it began, and at the latest 24 hours after it began; after that, the usual No current data rule applies, with its words and its notice. During a warm-up the trend arrow and the 5-minute delta are shown as unknown, and the display card and the wall panels show the words Sensor warming up in place of the glucose value, with no zone word. With No-data notice on, the notice is also sent during a warm-up, from 3 hours after it began while no reading has arrived: The sensor warm-up began at 7:15 AM and no reading has arrived since. A warm-up usually takes much less time than this. Check the CGM sensor and its app. A warm-up is normally much shorter than 24 hours. This method is a GlucoCraft rule.

• Restarts and outages. Each reading is saved when it is stored, and a Home Assistant restart or a loss of power does not discard stored readings. A reading that arrives while Home Assistant is shutting down or starting may not be stored. A value that a source shows again at the start is not taken as a new reading, so a source that has stopped still leads to No current data at the usual time. While Home Assistant is down nothing is recorded: the time remains a gap, and no reading is made up for it. After a gap, the trend remains unknown until sufficient new readings are available.
Statistics
<ul>

• Time weighting. Statistics are weighted by time, not by the number of readings. Each reading represents the interval until the next reading; when that interval is a gap ({gap_rule}), or for the most recent reading, it represents one reading interval, so that a gap does not extend the preceding value. The reading interval of a stretch is the median of the 10 intervals before the reading. This method is a GlucoCraft rule.

• Sensor active (data received by GlucoCraft) is determined from the readings GlucoCraft received: each reading represents the time until the next reading, so a shorter interval (for example a dropout of a few minutes) counts in full; before a gap (see {sec:gaps|Gaps, Reading Interval and No Current Data}), a reading represents only its own reading interval, and the rest of the gap counts as time without data. Sensor active is that time as a percentage of the period, the same time as in the time weighting. It is close to, but not the same as, the CGM system's own percentage of time the CGM is active: the CGM system counts the readings its sensor recorded, including readings that did not reach GlucoCraft (for example during an interruption in the delivery from the CGM system, its app or its cloud service, or a connection or network outage, or a time when Home Assistant was not running), and it applies its own rules to short dropouts. The two values can therefore differ; a lower value here usually means that readings did not reach GlucoCraft. The measure reflects data received, not sensor wear time. This method is a GlucoCraft rule.
  • Enough data (the 70% rule). A period's statistics (the time in ranges, the mean, the standard deviation, CV, GMI, GRI, the lowest and the highest value, and the weekly values, comparisons and summaries built from them) are shown only when sensor active is at least 70% of that period, compared before rounding. The 2019 international consensus gives 70% of the data of 14 days as the condition for its metrics {cite:battelino2019|Table 2}; GlucoCraft applies the same 70% to every period, from 6 hours to 6 months, on every page, display and report. This method is a GlucoCraft rule. Shown in any case: the current reading and its zone, the graphs, which show the readings received, and the time at the sensor's limit. The display card and the wall panels show --- for a value without enough data. The dashboard pages and the CGM Report show one note per period for all its values, for example Last 30 days: not enough data yet. GlucoCraft shows a period's statistics once the sensor has covered at least 70% of it. So far it has covered 23%. With no gaps, about 14 more days are needed. The time still needed is calculated when the page opens, from the length of the period and the time the readings received cover: it is the time the readings still have to cover to reach 70% of the period, in days, or in hours for the periods of 6 and 24 hours. It is an estimate: a gap makes it longer, and readings that leave the period at its start can make it longer as well.

• Readings at the sensor's limit (LO / HI) are left out of the mean, standard deviation, CV, GMI and the lowest and highest values, and counted as very low or very high in the time in ranges; their number and time are stated (see {sec:lohi|Readings Outside the Sensor's Range (LO / HI)}).
• Raw and smoothed values. All statistics use raw values. Smoothed values are used only for the trend arrow and the 5-minute delta, because smoothing reduces measured variability.

• Rolling periods. 6 hours, 24 hours, 7, 14, 30 and 90 days and 6 months (180 days; 180d in entity identifiers), each ending at the present time ("24 hours" denotes the preceding 24 hours, not the period since midnight). Periods are recalculated every 5 minutes.

• Change Over Time uses, for each of the last 26 week ends, the 14 days ending there, the period recommended by the consensus {cite:battelino2019}, and, as faint dots without comparison, the 7 days ending there; weeks are counted back from the present time and are not calendar weeks. The comparison table uses the last 4 weeks (28 days), 9–13 weeks ago and 22–26 weeks ago. A week or a 4-week period with less than 70% sensor active has no value (---, a gap in the line; see Enough data above); the differences and the direction are calculated for the periods with enough data, and the Sensor active row shows how much data each period has; GMI is shown only for periods of 14 days or more. Direction: the value of the last 4 weeks compared with the 4 weeks 22–26 weeks ago, or 9–13 weeks ago when 22–26 weeks ago does not have enough data; No change when the difference rounds to zero at one decimal; a numerical difference without clinical interpretation, and not the 4-week direction of the weekly pages. ‡ marks a difference in time in range of 5 percentage points or more in either direction between the two periods compared (consensus ranges only), not an assessment {cite:battelino2019|Table 3 note}. Calculated hourly. This method is a GlucoCraft rule.

• Calendar days are used only by the daily chart on Custom Ranges (while it exists) and by the CGM Report. The days and the night and day periods of the CGM Report and the daily removal of old readings follow Home Assistant's time zone, as does every time on the dashboard, the display cards and the wall panels (the clock, the graph axes, the banners and the readouts). Readings are stored with their measurement time, so a change of time zone changes where a day begins, not the readings.
Trend Arrow and 5-Minute Delta
<ul>

• Readings are smoothed with a moving average whose length depends on recent stability: 20 minutes when the range of the preceding 20 minutes is below 10 mg/dL (0.6 mmol/L), 15 minutes when it is below 25 mg/dL (1.4 mmol/L), and 10 minutes otherwise. The rate of change is the difference between this average and the average of the preceding window of the same length, per minute, limited to 3, 5 or 8 mg/dL per minute for the 20-, 15- and 10-minute windows; the trend category is taken from it in mg/dL per minute, rounded to one decimal. The 5-minute delta (5 MIN DELTA on the display card and wall panels) is its change over 5 minutes, in whole mg/dL or in mmol/L with one decimal. This method is a GlucoCraft rule.

• {ref:abbott|Abbott Diabetes Care} (2022) describes trend arrows that show the direction in which glucose is heading: rising or falling quickly, more than 2 mg/dL per minute; rising or falling, between 1 and 2 mg/dL per minute; and changing slowly, less than 1 mg/dL per minute {cite:abbott|p. 11}. This explains the categories of the Trend arrow entity, which GlucoCraft applies to its own calculated rate of change for every CGM (GlucoCraft rule). GlucoCraft's arrow is calculated from smoothed readings, so it can lag behind the CGM system's own arrow.

• The arrow and the 5-minute delta come from the same smoothed readings: the arrow from the rate of change over the adaptive 10- to 20-minute window, the delta from the change over the last 5 minutes. The delta therefore reacts sooner to a change of direction, and the arrow is steadier.

• GlucoCraft names the categories Rising Quickly, Rising, Changing Slowly, Falling and Falling Quickly and applies the thresholds in mg/dL; in mmol/L, 2 and 1 mg/dL per minute are 0.11 and 0.06 mmol/L per minute (converted by GlucoCraft). The display card and the wall panels write the trend word in sentence case, for example Falling quickly. With the setting Trend shown as set to Word, the TREND column shows this word instead of the arrow: the word is the broader category of the same rate, which the arrow shows in finer steps (a longer word on two lines).

• On the display card and the wall panels the arrow is turned in proportion to the rate of change, in steps of 4.5 degrees (the rate of change rounded to 0.1 mg/dL per minute), shown in whole degrees: horizontal for no change, 45 degrees at 1 mg/dL per minute, and straight up or down at 2 mg/dL per minute or more. The name under the arrow is the name of the source in use. This method is a GlucoCraft rule.
docs.section.lohi.title: Readings Outside the Sensor's Range (LO / HI)
docs.section.lohi.body: A CGM system measures glucose only within its measurement range. Below and above it, the system shows a text instead of a number, for example LO / HI, LOW / HIGH (translated in other languages, for example BAS / ÉLEVÉ) or Below 50 mg/dL / Above 400 mg/dL. Integrations pass such readings to Home Assistant in different forms: as the text, as a code (for example 39 for LOW and 401 for HIGH from the sharing service of Dexcom CGM systems) or as a number at or beyond the limit {cite:haCore,mulley2026,nightscoutCode,pydexcom}.
Measurement ranges
<table>
<tr><th>CGM system</th><th>mg/dL</th><th>mmol/L</th><th>Shown outside the range</th><th>Source</th></tr>
FreeStyle Libre 2 and 3 systems (United States, Canada)40–4002.2–22.2LO / HI({ref:abbottLlu}, {ref:abbott2025|2025})
FreeStyle Libre 2 and 3 systems (other countries)40–5002.2–27.8LO / HI{cite:abbottLlu}FreeStyle Libre 14 day system (United States)40–5002.2–27.8LO / HI{cite:abbott2021}
Dexcom G7 CGM system40–4002.2–22.2LOW / HIGH{cite:dexcomG7}
Medtronic Simplera system50–4002.8–22.2Below 50 mg/dL / Above 400 mg/dL{cite:medtronicSimplera}
Medtronic Guardian Connect system40–4002.2–22.2Below 40 mg/dL / Above 400 mg/dL{cite:medtronicGc}
Eversense E3 system40–4002.2–22.2LO / HI{cite:senseonics2023}
SIBIONICS GS1 CGM system40–4502.2–25.0Readings above 450 mg/dL are drawn at 450 in the app's graph{cite:sibionics2023}
Medtrum TouchCare Nano CGM40–4002.2–22.2Not stated in the source{cite:medtrum}

Examples only; the table is not a list of supported systems, and GlucoCraft does not identify the CGM model. The upper limit depends on the system and, for FreeStyle Libre systems, on the country, so it cannot be one constant; the lower limit is 40 mg/dL for most systems and 50 mg/dL for the Medtronic Simplera system. For any other system, its own documentation states the range.
How GlucoCraft recognizes a limit reading
<ul>
• Values in mmol/L are first converted to mg/dL (× 18.016).

• LO: the texts LO, LOW or Below … (and translations where an integration passes them), a value of 39 mg/dL (2.2 mmol/L) or less {cite:mulley2026,nightscoutCode}, or a value below the source's lower limit. With the lower limit Automatic, only a value below the limit is LO, because a sensor may measure the limit value itself. With the lower limit set by hand (40 or 50 mg/dL), a value at or below it is LO.

• HI: the texts HI, HIGH or Above …, exactly 401 from a source that uses the codes of Dexcom CGM systems {cite:mulley2026}, or a value beyond the source's upper limit. With the upper limit Automatic, only a value above the limit is HI, because a sensor may measure the limit value itself. With the upper limit set by hand (400, 450 or 500 mg/dL), a value at or above it is HI.
• "At the limit" is compared at the precision of the limits: whole mg/dL, or one decimal in mmol/L (40 and 50 mg/dL are 2.2 and 2.8 mmol/L; 400, 450 and 500 mg/dL are 22.2, 25.0 and 27.8 mmol/L).

• The reading is stored and marked as a limit reading (low or high). Each record of the readings file holds a number, so it holds the source's lower or upper limit (in mg/dL); that number is never used as a value.

• States that are not readings at all are not stored (see {sec:how|How GlucoCraft Is Designed}), among them 1–12 (error codes of Nightscout and of Dexcom CGM systems) {cite:nightscoutCode}, 38 (an error marker of xDrip+) {cite:xdrip}, warm-up markers (for example 65535 from some FreeStyle Libre integrations) and, from a Nightscout source, any value below 39 {cite:nightscoutCode}.
• This method is a GlucoCraft rule, built from the documented behavior of the integrations and systems above.
How a limit reading is shown
<ul>

• While the current reading is a limit reading, the display card and the wall panels show, in place of the glucose value, four lines in the layout of No current data: Very low or Very high, large, in the very-low or very-high color (by default dark red or dark blue); Below sensor range (LO) or Above sensor range (HI); since when the readings have been at the limit, with how long (Since 3:12 AM (2 h 5 min)); and the last measured value before them with its time (Last measured: 52 mg/dL at 3:10 AM). The TREND column stays blank, and the 5-minute delta shows ---. Since is the first reading of the current unbroken run of limit readings of the same kind; a data gap (see {sec:gaps|Gaps, Reading Interval and No Current Data}) starts a new run, and the start and the last measured value are kept across a restart. Without a new reading after the No current data after interval, the usual No current data screen follows, with Last reading: LO or Last reading: HI. The Statistics table on Consensus Ranges shows the text LO or HI instead of a number, followed by below the sensor's lower limit or above the sensor's upper limit and the zone word. The limit value is never shown as a measured value.

• On the graphs. A limit reading has no value, so no line is drawn to or from it. Instead, a row of small marks runs along the bottom edge of the graph (LO) or along its top edge (HI) for as long as the readings were beyond the sensor's range, in the very-low or very-high color. A stretch is an unbroken run of limit readings of the same kind; a measured reading, a reading beyond the other limit or a data gap ends it. The marks show when the readings were beyond the sensor's range, and on which side; they show no value. While the current reading is beyond the range, the screen in the value's place says so in words.

• Why at the edge, and not at a value. A limit reading tells only that glucose was below or above what the CGM sensor can measure. Drawn at the limit, for example at {value_40} or {value_400} {unit}, it would look like a measured value, and the true value can lie well beyond the limit. The edge of the graph stands for no particular number: it shows only the direction, below or above everything the graph shows. The calculations treat these readings the same way: they are left out of every calculated value and counted as very low or very high in the time in ranges (see Why limit readings are left out of the calculations and still counted in the time in ranges below).

• Marks and gaps. A break in the line without marks is a gap: no readings were received, so there are no data for that time (see {sec:gaps|Gaps, Reading Interval and No Current Data}). A break in the line with marks along the bottom or the top edge is not a gap: readings were received, and they lay beyond the sensor's range. The Statistics table, the notifications and the report state the period's time at the limit.

• Where. The marks are drawn on the glucose graphs of the display card and the dashboard, on the 6-hour graph and the period graphs of the wall panels, and in the glucose profile and the daily glucose profiles of the CGM Report (page and PDF). Color is not the only cue: the bottom edge stands for below the sensor's range and the top edge for above it; in the CGM Report, the letters LO and HI also name the side. This method is a GlucoCraft rule.
• The Statistics table, the notifications and the report state the number of limit readings and their time.

• sensor.glucocraft_last_glucose_reading is unknown during a limit reading, so that no limit value enters Home Assistant's history and statistics; its attributes limit (low, high or none) and limit_text (LO, HI or none) mark the limit reading, and value_mgdl then holds the stored limit for the wall panels, which is no measurement. The CSV export contains the same flag, with no number in glucose_mg_dl.
Why limit readings are left out of the calculations and still counted in the time in ranges

A limit reading tells only that glucose lies beyond what the CGM sensor can measure; it gives no value. GlucoCraft therefore never uses it as a number: mean glucose, standard deviation, CV, GMI, the lowest and highest values, the trend and the 5-minute delta come from the measured readings alone, and a period with limit readings alone shows --- for them. It still tells the range in which the reading lies, and that needs no number: a LO reading is below every range limit and a HI reading above every range limit. So it counts as very low or very high in the time in ranges, in the GRI and in the low-glucose events, where an event's lowest value can be LO, and its time counts as sensor active. Leaving it out of the time in ranges as well would remove the lowest and highest glucose of a period from the time below and above range.

This method is a GlucoCraft rule. The consensus statements on CGM metrics do not address readings outside the measurement range {cite:battelino2019,danne2017}, and others treat them in different ways: the FreeStyle Libre software shows sensor values below 40 mg/dL as 40 mg/dL and above 500 mg/dL as 500 mg/dL in its reports {cite:abbottSoftware}; a community cohort study replaced low and high messages with 39 and 401 mg/dL {cite:spartano2025}; and the statistical analysis plan of a clinical trial leaves values outside the reportable range out, because they are "not considered as reliable values" {cite:ultragenyx2024}. So a mean or a GMI in GlucoCraft can differ from a manufacturer's report on the same readings. The true value lies beyond the limit, so leaving such a reading out can make a mean lower than the true mean during HI readings and higher during LO readings; that is why the Statistics table, the notifications and the report state the time at the limit with these values.

As an example of how a manufacturer defines these readings, the FreeStyle Libre 3 system shows HI above 400 mg/dL and LO below 40 mg/dL. What to do when HI or LO appears is described in the instructions of each CGM system. {cite:abbottHiLo}
The very-low and very-high limits stay within the sensor's limits
<ul>

• The very-low limit of the ranges in the settings cannot be lower than the source's sensor lower limit, and the very-high limit cannot be higher than its sensor upper limit, each as in use (Automatic or the setting below). With a second source the stricter limits of the two apply: the higher lower limit and the lower upper limit. So a LO reading is always very low and a HI reading always very high, on the display card, the wall panels, the sensors, the statistics and the report.

• The Glucose ranges screen ({configure} > Glucose ranges, while the optional feature Custom ranges and goals is on) refuses a value outside the sensor's limits, in either unit, and compares at the precision it shows: the limit itself is accepted (40 mg/dL = 2.2 mmol/L).

• When the glucose source or a sensor limit setting is changed under {configure} > {screen_sources} and the new limits do not fit the very-low or very-high limit in the settings, the Glucose ranges screen follows, with the limit that does not fit marked; the source and the ranges are saved together once they fit. When a source shows its limit only later (Automatic) and a very-low or very-high limit in the settings no longer fits, GlucoCraft uses the sensor's limit for that one limit only, and a Home Assistant repair notice states the values; it closes by itself when the setting fits again. The other limits stay as set: a low limit at or below the sensor's lower limit then has no readings, because every reading below that limit is LO and counts as very low (the same at the high end). The defaults, {value_54} and {value_250} {unit}, fit every sensor limit.
• This method is a GlucoCraft rule.
Settings: sensor lower limit and sensor upper limit
<ul>

• One pair per glucose source ({screen_sources}). Sensor lower limit: Automatic (the default), 40 or 50 mg/dL (2.2 or 2.8 mmol/L). Sensor upper limit: Automatic (the default), 400, 450 or 500 mg/dL (22.2, 25.0 or 27.8 mmol/L). A change of a limit applies to readings received after it; stored readings are not changed.

• Automatic, upper limit: a limit the source shows itself (an Above … text that names 400, 450 or 500 mg/dL, or the same value in mmol/L, or the code 401 of Dexcom CGM systems, taken as 400 mg/dL; a plain HI or HIGH, or an Above … text with another number, shows no limit), the delivering integration (the Dexcom and CareLink integrations: 400 mg/dL) or the device reported by Nightscout {cite:haCore}; otherwise 500 mg/dL, so that a measured value up to 500 mg/dL is never turned into HI. A Dexcom CGM system read through another route (not the Dexcom integration and not a Nightscout that reports a Dexcom device) may not be recognized; then set Sensor upper limit to 400 mg/dL. Automatic, lower limit: 40 mg/dL, or 50 mg/dL when the source shows the Below 50 mg/dL text of Medtronic CGM systems or is the CareLink integration. A limit the source has shown is kept across restarts, until a Nightscout source reports another device.
• In use: {sensor_limits}. Listed on Settings Status.

• Sensor cap notice. When a source's readings repeatedly stop at exactly {value_400} or {value_450} {unit} and never exceed it, a Home Assistant repair notice suggests checking Sensor upper limit; with the upper limit set by hand to that value, readings at it are then shown as HI. In the same way, when the readings repeatedly stop at exactly {value_50} {unit} and never go below it (a source that sends its lower limit instead of LO), a repair notice suggests checking Sensor lower limit; with the lower limit set by hand to that value, readings at it are then shown as LO.
  • Readings at the limit in use as numbers. With Automatic, when a source's readings repeatedly stay at exactly the limit GlucoCraft uses for it (for example 500 mg/dL) and arrive as that number, not as HI or LO, they are shown as measured readings, and the repair notice Glucose source stays at its upper limit, …, as a number or Glucose source stays at its lower limit, …, as a number says that such a source can be set by hand to that limit; it closes by itself when the limit is set by hand.
  • Numbers beyond a limit set by hand. When a source sends a number below a sensor lower limit set by hand, or above a sensor upper limit set by hand, the reading is shown as LO or HI as set, and the repair notice Glucose source sends numbers below the sensor lower limit set by hand or Glucose source sends numbers above the sensor upper limit set by hand says that the CGM sensor's limit may differ from the setting. The codes 39 mg/dL, 2.2 mmol/L and 401 mg/dL are not counted. The notice closes when the setting is changed or Home Assistant restarts, and opens again with the next such number.
  • These notices are GlucoCraft rules; they never change a stored reading.

The sensor limits must match the CGM sensor's measurement range. GlucoCraft sets them from the source where it can and shows a Repairs notice when the readings point to a different limit; otherwise they are set by hand (the table and the automatic rules above). {limit_responsibility}
docs.section.gaps.title: Gaps, Reading Interval and No Current Data
docs.section.gaps.body: A gap is {gap_rule}. In use for the current source: {gap_minutes} minutes (reading interval {interval}). The reading interval is determined for each source from its readings (the median of the 10 intervals before a reading), so that a stretch of data is judged by the readings around it. Every graph (on the dashboard, the report page, the display card and the wall panels), the statistics (their time weighting) and sensor active judge each stretch with this same rule, so that they agree; the graphs and the panels calculate it from the readings they have. This method is a GlucoCraft rule; no consensus document defines the length of a data gap.

In every graph, a gap is shown as a break in the line: nothing is drawn across it. A shorter interval between two readings (for example a synchronization dropout of a few minutes) is not a gap: the graph joins the two readings with a straight line, and the statistics and sensor active count the time (the earlier reading represents it until the next reading). The values in between are not known: the line does not show measured values there. Across a gap, only the reading before it counts, for its own reading interval; the rest of the gap counts as time without data, also in sensor active.
Why 15 minutes, three reading intervals and per stretch

• 15 minutes. Some sources deliver part of their data at 15-minute steps, for example the history that some CGM systems deliver after a reconnection; and data delivered through a cloud service often have short synchronization dropouts of a few minutes. A shorter limit would interrupt the graphs and remove such intervals from the statistics, although readings exist on both sides.
• Three reading intervals. For a source with a longer interval, two missed readings in succession are not yet a gap.
• Per stretch, from the readings around each interval. The rule adapts when 1-minute readings follow 15-minute history, and when a second source has another interval.
• One rule. The same rule serves every graph, the statistics and sensor active, so that they describe the same data.

{interval_note} A source whose readings arrive every 15 minutes or less often (the median of its last 10 reading intervals) is not supported for live display, and the repair notice Glucose source is too slow for live display says so: the trend, the 5-minute delta and No current data do not work as intended with it, and the displays can show No current data between readings. Its readings are still stored and shown in the graphs. Setting No current data after to 30 minutes ({screen_sources}) reduces these messages, but a real interruption then takes up to 30 minutes to show. Occasional dropouts of a source that otherwise delivers every 5 minutes are not affected. The notice closes by itself when the readings arrive more often.

The limit. No current data means that the newest reading is older than the limit set under No current data after ({screen_sources}; 5 to 30 minutes, default 15 minutes; in use: {stale} minutes), that there is no reading yet, or that the newest reading is more than 5 minutes later than the system clock. GlucoCraft publishes this as one fact, binary_sensor.glucocraft_no_current_data; the dashboard, the display cards, the wall panels, the trend values and the summaries all follow it, and the display cards and the wall panels also count the age of the reading themselves, so that they show it while Home Assistant cannot reach them.

Why 15 minutes by default: it matches the gap rule, so that the status and the graphs agree. For comparison, the cited documentation of other CGM software and systems describes a stale-data warning after 15 minutes by default {cite:nightscout}; the last reading shown for 10.5 minutes and then a dash, followed by a Signal Loss message {cite:dexcomFaq}; and a Signal Loss message after 5 minutes without connection to the sensor, with a notification after 20 minutes where the Signal Loss alarm is on {cite:abbott2025}. GlucoCraft receives its data later than these systems (through their apps, cloud services and integrations), so a shorter limit would declare no current data during ordinary delivery delays. The default is a GlucoCraft rule.

What the screens show. While there is no current data, the trend arrow, the 5-minute delta and the in-range sensors are shown as unknown (the trend arrow and the 5-minute delta also during a sensor warm-up), and the dashboard shows the banner No Current Data, except during a sensor warm-up (when no readings are expected). Without a current reading the display card and the wall panels show words in place of the glucose value, never a number: No current data, or Sensor expired after the stated sensor expiry, and Sensor warming up during a sensor warm-up (also while a reading is still within the limit). No zone word is shown under them, the TREND column and the 5-minute delta show ---, and the status bar keeps the age of the reading (for example Reading: 2 h ago) and the status; the graphs keep the history. After the stated sensor expiry, while readings still arrive, the value and its zone word keep their zone color, the trend follows the readings, and the red status bar shows Sensor expiry passed. While the current reading lies beyond the sensor's range, the value's place shows the LO / HI screen (see {sec:lohi|Readings Outside the Sensor's Range (LO / HI)}).

A reading time ahead of the clock. While the newest reading's time is more than 5 minutes ahead of Home Assistant's clock, its age cannot be calculated: the status bar of the display card and the wall panels shows Reading: ---, and no time is shown under the words. The dashboard's Maintenance page then explains what happened and what to check (Home Assistant's clock and time zone; a reading time later than Home Assistant's clock is stored as the time the reading arrives, so neither the clock of the glucose source nor a source that sends its times without a time zone causes this), and the banner Reading Times Ahead of the Clock points to it (on Start, Today, Custom Ranges, Consensus Ranges and Maintenance).

The words throb. While there is no current reading, the words Sensor warming up, Sensor expired or No current data fade smoothly from full brightness to about 30% and back, once every 3 seconds, for the first 30 minutes of each episode without a current reading, so that its start is noticed; then they hold still and stay on screen for as long as the episode lasts. A new episode starts a new 30 minutes. The 30 minutes count from the age of the reading (during a warm-up, from its start), so a restart of a wall panel does not start them again. The words never disappear, and screen readers read the same text throughout. After the stated sensor expiry, the status bar's text Sensor expiry passed fades in the same way for as long as the expiry has passed, until a new sensor is recognized, without the 30-minute limit: it is small text in the status bar, and putting on a new sensor can take a while. The setting Fade the words when there is no current reading ({screen_displays}; on by default) turns both off on the display cards and the wall panels; the display cards also keep them still while the device's reduced-motion setting is on, so that a viewer without access to the settings can stop them as well. This method is a GlucoCraft rule.

The no-data notice (optional, off by default; {screen_notifications}). With No-data notice on, Home Assistant shows a notification once no reading has arrived for the time set under Notify after (15, 30, 60 or 120 minutes, default 30 minutes; never before no current data): GlucoCraft has received no readings since 1:02 AM. It is one notice for each interruption, during a sensor warm-up only from 3 hours after the warm-up began, with its own text (see {sec:how|How GlucoCraft Is Designed}, Sensor warm-up), removed when a reading arrives; it is not repeated, and no message follows when the readings return. The phones receive it only where No-data notice is selected under Notifications to send there, independently of the Home Assistant notice. It is a notice about GlucoCraft's data, never about glucose, and Home Assistant itself creates it: while Home Assistant is not running, it is not created.

Check Home Assistant. While a GlucoCraft notice is open in Home Assistant's Repairs (Settings > System > Repairs), the middle of the status bar on the display card and the wall panels also shows Check Home Assistant, taking turns every 3 seconds with Custom ranges or the warm-up text when one of them is shown. It never shows the notice's own text, which is read in Repairs, and nothing else on the screen changes; there is no sound and no message. It goes away when the notice closes, or when Ignore is chosen on the notice in Repairs. A wall panel offline and a failed CSV export are not Repairs notices: they are listed on Maintenance only.

Wall panels without Home Assistant. When a wall panel has had no connection to Home Assistant (its ESPHome connection) for an hour, or no successful download of GlucoCraft's data for an hour, everything below its clock and date is cleared to black, with: Cannot reach Home Assistant or load its data; since when, from whichever of the two problems began first, with how long (Since 9:41 PM (1 h 12 min)); the last reading with its time (Last reading: 112 mg/dL at 9:40 PM; while only the download fails, it keeps following new readings); and Check Home Assistant and the wall-panel address. The clock and the date stay: the panel keeps the time between synchronizations, and after a restart without Home Assistant they show --:-- until a time source has set the clock: Home Assistant, or a local time server where one is set in the panel's configuration (ntp_router). This screen takes the place of No current data, the warm-up and the LO / HI screen, does not throb, and swipes do nothing while it is shown. It clears by itself when both work again, to the screen that applies then (No current data, for example, while the sensor still sends nothing). Before the hour, a panel shows No current data after 15 minutes by its own count. What to check: that Home Assistant is running and the panel is connected to it (the panel's power and Wi-Fi; the panel in Settings > Devices & services > ESPHome), and that the id of the wall-panel address in the panel's configuration is the one shown on the screen {screen_displays} (see {sec:setup|Setup}, Wall panels, and {sec:troubleshooting|Troubleshooting}). The one-hour limit is a GlucoCraft rule.

The no-current-data limit and the gap rule are separate: the limit says whether the newest reading is current now and can be set; the gap rule decides whether a past stretch has data and is fixed, so that every installation gets the same statistics, sensor active and CGM Report.
docs.section.retention.title: Data Kept and CSV Export
docs.section.retention.body: Data kept
GlucoCraft keeps the readings of the last {retention} days (a fixed period). Older readings are removed once a day, as whole days at local midnight, so that the oldest stored day is always complete.

Why 200 days: the period covers everything GlucoCraft calculates: the 6-month report (180 days), the 90-day report with its previous period (180 days), the weekly pages of the display card and wall panels (26 weeks of 14-day values, 189 days) and Change Over Time (26 weeks). This method is a GlucoCraft rule.
What is not available
<ul>
• The 6-month report has no comparison with a previous period. It would require about 360 days of readings; no cited source asks for this comparison.

• Laboratory A1C results dated more than about 110 days ago show "no CGM comparison (data older than 200 days)": the comparison uses the GMI {cite:bergenstal2018} of the 90 days ending on the day of the test, that day included, which are no longer stored. This method is a GlucoCraft rule.

• Readings older than 200 days are not available to GlucoCraft. Home Assistant's own recorder history and long-term statistics of the GlucoCraft sensors are kept by Home Assistant under its own settings.
CSV export
<ul>

• How. Save CSV export on Maintenance, or the action glucocraft.export_csv, saves every stored reading as a CSV file in the folder glucocraft_exports of the Home Assistant configuration. The last 12 exports are kept; older export files are removed. A status line under the button shows the result.

• Content. One row per reading, oldest first, with the columns local_time (ISO 8601 with the UTC offset, in Home Assistant's time zone), utc_time, glucose_mg_dl (one decimal; empty for a LO / HI reading, which has no value), glucose_display (the value in the display unit as GlucoCraft shows it; a LO / HI reading as LO or HI), display_unit, source (primary, secondary, or empty for readings stored before the source was recorded) and limit (low, high or empty), in a file named glucocraft-readings_<date>_<time>.csv. Where laboratory A1C results have been entered, a second file, glucocraft-lab-a1c_<date>_<time>.csv, holds them (columns date, a1c_percent, a1c_mmol_mol and entered_unit: each result in both units, a result entered in percent converted to mmol/mol with the IFCC–NGSP master equation {cite:hoelzel2004}, and the unit it was entered in, percent or mmol_mol, in which the import reads it). Numbers use a decimal point, whatever the Decimal separator setting, so that other software can read them; the text is UTF-8. The action returns the folder, the file names and the number of readings, and a Home Assistant notification, GlucoCraft export, confirms the export.
• Why. The readings remain available outside GlucoCraft, for example before the oldest days are removed or for other software.

• Privacy. The files contain glucose data. The folder is not accessible from the web; it can be reached only through access to the Home Assistant configuration (for example a file-access add-on or a network share).
CSV import
<ul>

• How. The action glucocraft.import_csv (Developer tools > Actions; administrators) reads one of GlucoCraft's own readings exports back in, named by its file name in the folder glucocraft_exports (a file copied in from elsewhere is put into that folder first); without a name, the newest export there. The laboratory A1C results of the export with the same time stamp are read with it. An export in either display unit is read, also after a spreadsheet program saved it again with the decimal comma.

• Stored data win. A reading within 30 seconds of a stored reading is not imported: a stored reading is never changed or doubled. A laboratory result of a date already stored is kept as it is. Only readings within the {retention} days that GlucoCraft keeps are imported; a row that is not a plausible reading is left out. This method is a GlucoCraft rule.

• Result. A Home Assistant notification, GlucoCraft import, states how many readings were imported, how many were already stored, how many lay outside the days kept and how many rows could not be read, and how many laboratory results were imported; the action returns the same counts. The statistics, the report and the displays include the imported readings at once.

• Why. CSV exports copied out of the folder glucocraft_exports before GlucoCraft was deleted can be read back in after a reinstall (deleting GlucoCraft deletes the exports in that folder; see {sec:install|Installing, Updating and Removing GlucoCraft}).
docs.section.pages.title: Pages
docs.section.pages.body: <table>
<tr><th>Page</th><th>Content</th><th>Ranges</th></tr>

Start (titled GlucoCraft)The display card (the screens of a wall panel: square or rectangular, see {sec:setup|Setup}) and, beside it, a card with a row for each page and buttons for Maintenance, Settings Status and Documentation; the Maintenance button shows the Maintenance status, green with a wrench and No issues, or red with a warning icon and the number of issues. Both cards have the same height and are stacked on narrow screens.—
TodayStatistics and glucose graphs for 6 hours to 14 days.Consensus

Custom RangesBased on the ranges and goals in the settings: the box Differences from the Consensus Ranges; the core measures (time in tight range, time in range, the time below the low and the very-low limit and the time above the high limit) for the last 14 days with the custom goals, ✓ / ✗ and their change; statistics for seven periods with the goals, Change Over Time with each goal, and graphs for 14 days to 6 months, with a chart of the daily mean, lowest and highest reading of the last 14 days. The page exists only while the optional feature Custom ranges and goals is on (see {sec:setup|Setup}); its row on Start is shown only while custom ranges or goals are set.Settings

Consensus RangesA headline card; the core measures (time in range, time in tight range, below 70, below 54 and above 180 mg/dL; 3.9, 3.0 and 10.0 mmol/L) for the last 14 days, with ✓ / ✗ and their change; Change Over Time of these five measures over 26 weeks, with the consensus target cited beside each measure; behind Show All Statistics: the Last Reading block, the statistics for seven periods, each with its consensus target and source, the comparison table (the last 4 weeks compared with 9–13 and 22–26 weeks ago: higher, lower or no change) and Change Over Time of seven further measures.Consensus

CGM ReportThe CGM Report shows the standardized metrics and glucose profile recommended for the Ambulatory Glucose Profile {cite:battelino2019,bergenstal2013}. The 14-day summary and, for 30 days, 90 days or 6 months, a longer-term overview in consecutive 14-day periods; hypoglycemia events; laboratory A1C compared with GMI; PDF, optional printing and two optional appendices (see Report and PDF below). Full days ending at the last midnight.Consensus

MaintenanceMaintenance issues, shown while there are issues or while the newest reading's time is ahead of the clock, each with where it is resolved: a wall panel offline for 10 minutes or more, an open GlucoCraft issue in Home Assistant's Repairs, and a failed CSV export (until an export succeeds or GlucoCraft restarts); no current data and the sensor expiry are not counted, as the banners and the status headline show them. While the newest reading's time is more than 5 minutes ahead of Home Assistant's clock, the page's first card explains what happened, what it means and what to check. Then sources (reading interval and gap threshold), sensor, the CSV export, trend arrow calculation and wall panels (type, status, uptime and firmware version of each connected panel, or a note that none is connected).—

Settings StatusAll settings in use, the consensus defaults and the requirements of each setting; the Change Settings button opens GlucoCraft in Settings > Devices & services, where Configure opens the settings.—
DocumentationThis page.—

Each page except the Documentation has About This Page, which describes the content and the calculation, at its end, before the page footer. The footer of every page carries the line For development and testing only. Not for medical use. with a link to the {sec:disclaimer|Disclaimer} and the license line; the footer of every page except the CGM Report and the Documentation also carries a color key where the page uses colors and the source of the targets and ranges. On Consensus Ranges and, while it exists, Custom Ranges, further measures and periods are behind the Show All Statistics button at the bottom of the page.
Report and PDF
<ul>

• Periods. 14 days, 30 days, 90 days or 6 months, as full days ending at the last midnight. The first section always shows the most recent 14 days, the period recommended by the cited sources {cite:bergenstal2013,battelino2019}.

• Summary or full report. The summary contains the 14-day section with its daily glucose profiles, the longer-term overview (30 days and longer), the weekly trend of the last 26 weeks (90 days and 6 months), Hypoglycemia, Hyperglycemia, the comparison with the previous period (not for 6 months), Data Quality and laboratory A1C. The full report adds Hypoglycemia Events by Period (one table: for each period of 14, 30 and 90 days and 6 months within the report period, its sensor active, the level 1 events, those that reached level 2, the events per day, the median and the longest duration and the event starts by time of day and at night), the daily glucose profiles of the whole period (30 days and longer), Daily Patterns, the Daily Summary, the Daily Log (one row per day, one column per hour) and the Monthly Summary, which covers every calendar month of the report period. Both end with About This Report, the appendices that were chosen, the references and License.

• Layout. Every section opens with a caption line that names its rule and source, shows its data and ends with Notes, which explain them with their sources; in the PDF, Notes that reach the next page continue there under the section's title. About This Report describes the general method: the data sources, the report period, the data and their gaps, the readings at the sensor's limit and the rounding. The Longer-Term Overview also shows the lowest and the highest measured value of the period.

• Glucose sources. Every page of the PDF names the glucose sources in its header, each by its name in Home Assistant (else its entity id), and About This Report names them as well; with a second source it states how the second source fills gaps and the share of the period's readings that came from it. The report prints the names of the glucose sources. To keep a personal name off the report, rename the source in Home Assistant.
• Colors. The time-in-ranges colors of the published report examples: very low dark red, low red, in range green, tight range light green, high yellow, very high orange {cite:battelino2019,idc2024}.

• PDF. Download PDF creates the selected report in color or grayscale; the color choice applies to the PDF and the printout only. Each PDF is also kept in the folder glucocraft_reports of the Home Assistant configuration (the last 12), which is not accessible from the web. Times, dates, numbers and the units follow the Time format, Date format, Decimal separator, Display unit and A1C and GMI unit settings; the paper follows PDF paper size and the calendar weeks (the rows of the daily glucose profiles and the monthly calendars) First day of the week.

• Printing (optional). With an address in the Report printer setting ({screen_report}), Print Report or the action glucocraft.print_report sends the PDF to a network printer that accepts PDF over the Internet Printing Protocol (IPP); Print Report prints two-sided where the printer supports it. The action takes the period (days: 14, 30, 90 or 180; default 14; another number is refused with the error This report period is not available: 60 days. The CGM Report can be created for 14, 30, 90 or 180 days. Check the card's or automation's settings., and no report is created), report (summary or full; default summary), color (on: color; off: grayscale; on by default), two_sided (two-sided printing where the printer supports it; on by default) and the two appendix fields. After each attempt the Home Assistant notification GlucoCraft CGM Report states the result. Without a printer address, no PDF is created and the action fails. ipps:// and https:// work only with a printer certificate that Home Assistant trusts; most printers' own certificates are not trusted, and the print then fails.

• Laboratory A1C. Results are entered in percent or mmol/mol, on the page or with the action glucocraft.add_lab_a1c (a result in mmol/mol is kept in whole mmol/mol and converted to percent with the IFCC–NGSP master equation {cite:hoelzel2004}); a result with the same date replaces the earlier one, and glucocraft.remove_lab_a1c removes the result of a date. Results are shown in the A1C and GMI unit setting; each result is compared with the GMI {cite:bergenstal2018} of the 90 days ending on the day of the test (that day included), shown only with at least 70% sensor active {cite:battelino2019}. A result dated more than about 110 days ago has no CGM comparison (see {sec:retention|Data Kept and CSV Export}). The ADA Standards of Care state that the comparability of A1C and mean CGM glucose depends on the number of days of CGM wear, the timing of the A1C test relative to the CGM period, the accuracy of the meter and the CGM system, the lag between interstitial and venous glucose, and factors that affect A1C or red blood cell turnover {cite:ada2026|Correlation Between A1C and Blood Glucose Monitoring and Continuous Glucose Monitoring section, para. 2}. This explains why a laboratory result and the GMI of the 90 days before it can differ; the 90-day period is a GlucoCraft rule. In the data from which GMI was derived, the GMI and the laboratory A1C differed by 0.3 percentage points or more in 51% of 528 participants and by 0.5 percentage points or more in 28% {cite:bergenstal2018|Table 3}. This explains why the laboratory results in this section can differ from the GMI shown beside them.
• Previous period. The 14-day, 30-day and 90-day reports compare the period with the one before it; the 6-month report has no previous period (see {sec:retention|Data Kept and CSV Export}).

• Appendices (optional, off by default). Selected on the page or with the action fields include_custom_appendix and include_research_appendix; each is added to the page, the PDF and the printout. Custom Ranges and Goals shows the statistics calculated with the ranges and goals in the settings, labeled as the user's own settings; it is available only while the optional feature Custom ranges and goals is on. Measures Defined for Research shows measures that the 2023 consensus defines for clinical trials and for which no clinical-care definition or target exists {cite:battelino2023}: the number, the total duration and the longest of the extended high-glucose events; it has no targets, colors or comparisons, and GlucoCraft's method is listed in the appendix.

• Enough data. The values of a period, also of a week or a day, are shown only with at least 70% sensor active (see {sec:how|How GlucoCraft Is Designed}, Enough data); otherwise the report gives the period's sensor active, a dash (-) in place of its values, and a note with the reason and, for the report's periods, about how much longer it takes with no gaps.
  • Readings at the sensor's limit are left out of the values and the glucose curves, counted in the time in ranges and the events, and their number and time are stated under the statistics (see {sec:lohi|Readings Outside the Sensor's Range (LO / HI)}).

docs.section.ranges.body: Consensus ranges
<table>
<tr><th>Range</th><th>mg/dL</th><th>mmol/L</th><th>Source</th></tr>
Very low (level 2)below 54below 3.0{cite:battelino2019}
Low (level 1)54–693.0–3.8{cite:battelino2019}
In range70–1803.9–10.0{cite:battelino2019}
Tight range70–1403.9–7.8{cite:battelino2023}
High (level 1)181–25010.1–13.9{cite:battelino2019}
Very high (level 2)above 250above 13.9{cite:battelino2019}

The 2019 international consensus names the glucose ranges of the standardized report "Very High" (level 2), "High" (level 1), "Low" (level 1) and "Very Low" (level 2) {cite:battelino2019|Standardization of CGM Data Presentation section, para. 1}. This explains the range names Very high, High, Low and Very low.
Today, Consensus Ranges and the main sections of the CGM Report always use these ranges, irrespective of the ranges in the settings, so that values can be compared with the published targets.
Ranges in the settings

{ranges_in_use} The cited consensus also publishes targets for other groups; they are not included (see {sec:metrics|Metrics and Sources}, Other groups). While the optional feature Custom ranges and goals is on, the ranges in the settings determine the color and the zone word of the glucose value, the range bands of the graphs and the statistics under the graphs on the display card and the wall panels (marked Custom ranges in the status bar while they differ from the consensus ranges) and the content of Custom Ranges; while it is off, the consensus ranges are used for all of these. They are not used on Today, Consensus Ranges or the main sections of the CGM Report; its optional appendix Custom Ranges and Goals shows the statistics calculated with them. While the ranges in use differ from the consensus ranges, each period of the summaries also states its time in, below and above the custom ranges (see {sec:notifications|Notifications (Not Alarms)}). The very-low limit cannot be lower than the glucose sensor's lower limit and the very-high limit not higher than its upper limit, so that a LO reading is always very low and a HI reading always very high (see {sec:lohi|Readings Outside the Sensor's Range (LO / HI)}).
{custom_note}
Mean glucose, standard deviation, CV and GMI do not depend on range limits and are identical under either set of ranges.
Terminology
<ul>
• {standard_statement} A goal set by the user is labeled Custom goal. {no_default_goals}
• Comparisons with a target or goal are reported only as met or not met (✓ / ✗, green / red), an arithmetic comparison. GlucoCraft does not grade values or describe them as favorable or unfavorable.

• 4-week direction (Increasing, Decreasing, Stable; weekly pages of the display card and wall panels). The mean of the weekly 14-day values of the last 4 weeks is compared with the mean of the 4 weeks before. A difference of more than 2% of the chart scale of the page (for example 1 percentage point on the time-in-range page, scale 50–100%) is Increasing or Decreasing; a smaller difference is Stable. It needs at least one weekly value in each of the two 4-week blocks and a weekly value 8 or more weeks back. This method is a GlucoCraft rule. The direction describes numerical change only and carries no clinical interpretation; it is not the 5-percentage-point change that the 2023 consensus considers clinically meaningful {cite:battelino2023}.
• Direction (Change Over Time on the dashboard) is another GlucoCraft rule with a similar name: it compares the last 4 weeks with 22–26 or 9–13 weeks ago (see {sec:how|How GlucoCraft Is Designed}).

• Green and red as a result (a value, a mark or a headline) are shown only where a consensus target (or, on Custom Ranges while it exists, a goal in the settings) exists, and only for periods of at least 14 days with at least 70% sensor active, as recommended by the consensus {cite:battelino2019}. Shorter periods are shown without color. On the Change Over Time charts and the weekly pages, the green and red background marks the target or goal on the chart's scale, whatever the data; it is not a result.
Colors

Each page that uses these colors ends with a one-line key listing only the colors of that page, with a link to this table. Custom Ranges exists only while the optional feature Custom ranges and goals is on.
<table>
<tr><th>Color</th><th>Meaning</th></tr>

GreenMet: the consensus target cited beside the value (or the custom goal, on Custom Ranges); a reading received within the No current data after interval (status bar, Maintenance; the status bar shows the age of the reading); a CSV export saved (Maintenance); no maintenance issues (the Maintenance button on Start); the part of a Change Over Time chart or a weekly page within the target or goal (not a result).

RedNot met: the cited consensus target (or the custom goal); no current data; sensor expired; a CSV export not saved (Maintenance); maintenance issues (the Maintenance button on Start and Maintenance issues on Maintenance); the part of such a chart outside the target or goal (not a result).

AmberSensor expiry within 24 hours (status bar, banner and the Maintenance headline); second source in use (banner); a period without enough data yet (less than 70% sensor active); a CSV export in progress (Maintenance).
PurpleWaiting: sensor warm-up in progress, or no data received yet.

Neutral grayChart background where no target or goal exists for the measure. GrayThe status bar of the display card and the wall panels, and the headline of Maintenance, while the status has no color (for example while GlucoCraft is loading). Label grayThe small value of the square wall panel's weekly pages (---) without a current reading, in the gray of the labels (#888888 on black; with the Home Assistant theme, the theme's secondary text color). Light grayThe lowest to the highest reading in the graphs of 24 hours to 6 months and in the daily chart on Custom Ranges (the white line or dots are the means).

The CGM Report uses the time-in-ranges colors instead (dark red, very low; red, low; green, in range; light green, tight range; yellow, high; orange, very high), the colors of the published report examples it follows, so they differ from the display colors below; it also uses a gray band for the range 70–180 mg/dL (3.9–10.0 mmol/L) in its graphs and hourly log, and, on the report page, amber for data warnings (see {sec:pages|Pages}, Report and PDF).

The top cards of Consensus Ranges and, while it exists, Custom Ranges, and their rows on Start, are green (✓) or red (✗) according to the 14-day time in range compared with the consensus target or the goal, and carry no color with less than 70% sensor active. Today and its row carry no color, because periods shorter than 14 days are not compared with targets {cite:battelino2019}.
Weekly Pages of the Display Card and Wall Panels

The nine weekly pages show the 14-day values at the end of each of the last 26 weeks, with the 4-week direction (see Terminology). A weekly value is shown when its 14 days have at least 70% sensor active (see {sec:how|How GlucoCraft Is Designed}, Enough data); a week with less data is a gap in the line. The date under the chart marks the middle of each point's 14-day window (7 days before its end), and every fourth week is dated. This method is a GlucoCraft rule. They use one of two range sets: the consensus ranges or the custom ranges. The range set is selected once in the settings ({configure} > {screen_displays} > Range set of the weekly pages) for the display card and every wall panel together: the consensus ranges with the consensus targets (default), or the custom ranges with the custom goals (offered only while custom ranges or goals are set). The line under each title, the target line and the green and red background follow the range set shown; where a target or goal colors the chart, its top right says whose it is (Consensus target or Custom goal), and a page without one has a neutral gray chart and no label. GlucoCraft sends both range sets to the display card and the panels, which show the selected one; there is no switch on the panels. The dashboard shows the consensus ranges on Consensus Ranges and, while the optional feature Custom ranges and goals is on, the custom ranges on Custom Ranges.
Display Colors of the Glucose Value

The glucose value on the display cards and any wall panels is colored by the range the value falls in, in the display colors of the settings ({screen_displays}). The default palette shows lows in red and highs in blue: with the default ranges, dark red and red are the consensus very low and low ranges, blue and dark blue the consensus high and very high ranges {cite:battelino2019}, green the tight range {cite:battelino2023}, and amber the rest of the consensus in-range interval (70–180 mg/dL, 3.9–10.0 mmol/L). The bands of the graphs (on the display card, the wall panels and the dashboard's graphs) have colors of their own, the graph range colors of the settings; by default the time-in-ranges colors of the CGM Report, which follow the published report examples {cite:idc2024}. The bands are drawn at 60% over the graphs' black background. Any other color can be chosen for each range, in both sets. Each color band is a range in the settings; GlucoCraft adds no bands of its own. GlucoCraft publishes the colors in use as the attributes zone_colors and band_colors of sensor.glucocraft_configuration, and the color of the current value as zone_color of sensor.glucocraft_last_glucose_reading; the display card, the dashboard and the wall panels take them from there.

{colors_table}
{colors_caption}
Color Is Never the Only Cue
<ul>

• Zone word. The display card and the wall panels name the range of every value under it, in every setting: Very low, Low, In range, Tight range, High or Very high. The setting Trend shown as chooses only whether the TREND column shows the arrow or the trend word (see {sec:setup|Setup}). Without a current reading no value and no word under it are shown: the words No current data, Sensor expired or Sensor warming up take the value's place; during a reading beyond the sensor's range, Very low or Very high with Below sensor range (LO) or Above sensor range (HI); after the stated sensor expiry, while readings still arrive, the value and its zone word keep their zone color.
• Marks and words. Met and not met are shown as ✓ and ✗ with their words; the status is shown in words (No current data, Sensor expired, Warm-up, Sensor expiry passed, Check Home Assistant).

• Graphs. The graphs show the glucose values on a numbered axis; the range bands lie in a fixed order, from very low at the bottom to very high at the top. The graphs of the display card and the wall panels draw no lines at the range limits. The charts of Change Over Time name the target or goal under their title and mark it with a labeled line where it lies within the chart's scale, and the dashboard's glucose graphs have a key that names each band's limits. Readings beyond the sensor's range are marked along the bottom (LO) or the top (HI) edge of a graph (see {sec:lohi|Readings Outside the Sensor's Range (LO / HI)}).

• Color vision. Some colors of the default palettes can look alike with a color vision deficiency (for example, with deuteranopia, the red of the low range and the green of the tight range). The zone word, the marks and the status words carry the same information, also with colors chosen in the settings (see {sec:accessibility|Accessibility}).

• Range as text. The range is also published as text on sensor.glucocraft_last_glucose_reading: the attribute zone (very_low … very_high) in every zone; the attribute display_word, the zone word the displays show under the value (in every zone, In range and Tight range included; empty without current data and during a sensor warm-up; Sensor limit during a limit reading; after the stated sensor expiry it follows the data); and the attribute zone_label, the zone word outside the range only (Very low, Low, High, Very high), with no value inside the range.
